title: Present perfect and past 2 (I have done and I did)
subtitle: I have done and I did
summary: Choose the present perfect for a period that continues until now, and the past simple for a time that is finished.

lesson.heading: A finished time needs the past simple
lesson.text: We do not use the present perfect (I have done) when we talk about a finished time - for example **yesterday / last year / ten minutes ago**. We use a past tense.

examples.text: Paul and Lucy **arrived** ten minutes ago.
**Did you eat** a lot of sweets when you were a child?
I **got** home late last night. I **was** very tired and **went** straight to bed.

lesson.heading: When ... ? and What time ... ?
lesson.text: Use the past simple to ask **When ... ?** or **What time ... ?** These questions are about a point in the past, so the present perfect is not possible.

left.label: Present perfect
left.text: The past action is connected with now.
examples: Tom **has lost** his key. He can't get into the house.
Is Carla here or **has she left**?

right.label: Past simple
right.text: The action happened at a finished time.
examples: Tom **lost** his key yesterday. He couldn't get into the house.

left.label: Present perfect (have done)
left.text: A period of time that continues until now: today / this week / since 2010.
examples: **I've done** a lot of work today.
**Have you seen** Anna this morning? (it is still morning now)
**Have you seen** Ben recently? (in the last few days or weeks)
**I've been working** here since 2010. (I still work here now)

right.label: Past simple (did)
right.text: A finished time in the past: yesterday / last week / from 2010 to 2014.
examples: **I did** a lot of work yesterday.
**Did you see** Anna this morning? (it is now afternoon or evening)
**I worked** here from 2010 to 2014. (I don't work here now)

lesson.heading: Still true now, or over?
lesson.text: Ask yourself whether the situation continues to the present. If it does, use the present perfect. If it is over, use the past simple.

examples.text: I don't know where Lisa is. **I haven't seen** her. (= I haven't seen her recently)
*A:* Was Lisa at the party on Sunday? *B:* I don't think so. **I didn't see** her.
**We've been waiting** for an hour. (we are still waiting now)
**We waited** (or were waiting) for an hour. (we are no longer waiting)
Jack lives in Los Angeles. **He has lived** there for seven years.
Jack **lived** in New York for ten years. Now he lives in Los Angeles.

lesson.heading: never, and the end of a holiday
lesson.text: **I've never ridden a horse** means never in my life, up to now. **I never rode a bike when I was a child** is about a finished period. Compare what you say on the last day of a holiday and after you come back.

examples.text: **I've never ridden** a horse. (in my life)
**I never rode** a bike when I was a child.
Last day of your holiday: **It's been** a really good holiday. **I've really enjoyed** it.
After you come back: **It was** a really good holiday. **I really enjoyed** it.

lesson.text: If the sentence names a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 1999, ten minutes ago, when I was a child) or asks When ... ?, the present perfect is not possible - use the past simple.

exercises.statement: I've lost my key. I can't find it anywhere.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The key is still lost now, so the present perfect connects the past action with the present.

exercises.statement: Have you eaten a lot of sweets when you were a child?
exercises.explanation: Did you eat a lot of sweets when you were a child? 'When you were a child' is a finished time, so use the past simple.

exercises.prompt: Does each time expression describe a period that continues until now (present perfect) or a finished time (past simple)?
Paul and Lucy ___ about ten minutes ago.
exercises.explanation: 'Ten minutes ago' is a finished time: past simple.

exercises.prompt: Make a sentence: (the weather / be / cold / recently)
exercises.answer: The weather has been cold recently.
exercises.explanation: 'Recently' covers a period up to now, so the present perfect is used.
'Last night' is finished: I didn't sleep.

exercises.prompt: Mary lives in Dublin. ___ there all her life.
exercises.explanation: She still lives there, so the period continues until now: She has lived.

exercises.prompt: Make a question: (you / have / a holiday recently?)
exercises.answer: Have you had a holiday recently?
exercises.explanation: 'Recently' = in the last few weeks up to now, so use the present perfect.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct? 'My grandfather died before I was born. ___ him.' / 'I don't know Karen's husband. ___ him.'
options: I never met / I've never met
I've never met / I never met
I never met / I never met
exercises.explanation: The grandfather's life is a finished time (I never met him). Karen's husband is alive, so the period continues (I've never met him).

exercises.prompt: It's nearly lunchtime, and ___ Martin all morning. I wonder where he is.
exercises.explanation: It is still morning, so the period is unfinished: I haven't seen him.

exercises.statement: When has this bridge been built?
exercises.explanation: When was this bridge built? Questions with When ... ? take the past simple.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Where do you live? *B:* In Boston. *A:* How long ___ there? *B:* Five years. *A:* Where ___ before that? *B:* In Chicago.
options: have you lived / did you live
did you live / have you lived
do you live / did you live
exercises.explanation: Living in Boston continues now (have you lived / have you been living); Chicago is finished (did you live).
